input.question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?
input.ground_truth: > but I have no idea to estimate how many pixels are actually being lit up by CMBR. Zero. And very little of the overall noise is due to CMBR Thermal noise is a much much larger contributor than CMBR (by a factor of between 100 and 1,000) to the 'snowy' picture on analog televisions. In [this](_URL_0_) thread /u/MrDerpleton provides some great information on how the 'snow' pattern becomes rendered.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

I am a woman.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your old TV, when you don’t get a signal, and you see lots of little dots and fuzzy stuff — that’s called “snow.”

Now, some of that “snow” is because the TV is trying to find a signal but can’t. But a *tiny, tiny* bit of that fuzz comes from something called the “cosmic microwave background radiation.” 

This is a very, very faint “glow” left over from when the universe was very, very young. It’s like a super old leftover heat from the Big Bang, and it’s everywhere in space, even in your living room!

But here’s the important part: this cosmic background is so, so weak that you can’t see it on your TV at all. It’s like trying to see a single grain of sand in a whole swimming pool — it’s there, but it’s way too tiny to notice among all the other fuzz from the TV.

So, if you look at the “snow” on your TV, almost *none* of it is from the cosmic microwave background. All the snow is from the TV not finding a signal, not from space!
